title: Elevator Scheduling
description: Compare FCFS, SCAN, LOOK, and destination dispatch scheduling algorithms. Analyze mathematical optimization of wait time vs travel time tradeoffs.

segments.text: An elevator serving a forty-story building receives requests from multiple floors simultaneously. The scheduling algorithm determines average wait time — the difference between a twenty-second wait and a two-minute wait. Real elevator companies like Otis and ThyssenKrupp spend millions optimizing these algorithms because tenant satisfaction directly affects building lease rates.

First Come First Served: serve requests in arrival order. Elevator on floor 1, gets requests for floors 30, 5, 25, 3. It goes 1→30→5→25→3. Total travel: twenty-nine plus twenty-five plus twenty plus twenty-two equals ninety-six floors. Terrible efficiency — the elevator constantly reverses direction. Simple but only acceptable for very low traffic.

SCAN — the elevator algorithm — moves in one direction, serving all requests along the way, then reverses. Like a disk arm sweep. From floor 1 going up: serve 3, 5, 25, 30, then reverse. Total travel: twenty-nine plus twenty-seven equals fifty-six floors. Forty percent improvement over FCFS. But it always goes to the top before reversing, even if nobody is above floor 30.

LOOK improves on SCAN by only going as far as the highest request, not the top floor. Same requests: serve 3, 5, 25, 30, reverse from 30 instead of floor 40. Then descend to the lowest pending request. This eliminates unnecessary travel past the last request in each direction. Most real elevators use LOOK or a variant.

It's 8:45 AM in a fifty-story office building. Everyone is going up from the lobby. LOOK works well here. But at 6 PM, everyone is going down from various floors. The optimal strategy is different. How would you adapt the algorithm to traffic patterns?
segments.thought_prompt: How would you optimize elevator scheduling for morning rush (all going up) vs evening rush (all going down)?

segments.text: Destination dispatch asks riders to input their destination floor before boarding. The system groups people going to similar floors into the same elevator. Five people going to floors 20-25 get elevator A. Three people going to floors 35-40 get elevator B. This reduces stops per trip by thirty to forty percent compared to conventional dispatching.

The mathematical optimization is a variant of the Traveling Salesman Problem — NP-hard in general. But elevator constraints simplify it: movement is one-dimensional and direction changes are expensive. Dynamic programming can optimize within a single direction sweep. The objective function balances average wait time — how long until the elevator arrives — against travel time — how long the ride takes.

Wait time and travel time are often in conflict. Stopping at every floor minimizes wait time for new passengers but maximizes travel time for existing passengers. Express zones — floors 1-20 and 21-40 served by different elevators — reduce this conflict. The Petronas Towers use sky lobbies with express elevators to handle one hundred sixteen floors efficiently.

SCAN can starve requests at extreme floors. A request at floor 40 waits while the elevator repeatedly serves floors 1-20 during peak traffic. Anti-starvation measures: set a maximum wait time — if any request waits over sixty seconds, prioritize it regardless of direction. This prevents worst-case wait times at the cost of slightly higher average wait times.

Design a scheduling algorithm for a hospital elevator system. Requirements: emergency calls must preempt all other requests, patient transport has priority over visitor traffic, and maximum wait time must never exceed ninety seconds. How would you modify LOOK?
segments.thought_prompt: Design elevator scheduling for a hospital with emergency preemption and 90-second max wait guarantee.

segments.text: Elevator scheduling progresses from FCFS through SCAN and LOOK to destination dispatch. Each step trades simplicity for efficiency. The key tradeoff is wait time versus travel time, with anti-starvation guarantees preventing worst-case scenarios. In a design interview, show you understand the optimization landscape — not just the algorithms but when each one is appropriate.
